text.text: Cross-national research has consistently documented sociodemographic gradients in depression across European countries.
Most comprehensive analyses, however, predate the COVID-19 pandemic and its far-reaching consequences for population mental health and social hardship.

Using data from the European Social Survey Round 11 (ESS 11, collected in 2023(ESS 11, collected in  -2024)), the most recent wave to include a measure of depression (CES-D 8), we examined the social patterning of depressive symptoms across 22 EU countries and the UK (N = 39,645) using multilevel modelling with sample design weighting.
We confirm findings from prior ESS rounds of consistent gender, age, and income gradients in depression, confirming their persistence in the post-pandemic period.

Women reported higher depressive symptoms than men across all countries, and income emerged as the strongest individual-level predictor, with those in the lowest income tertile scoring on average 2.09 points higher on the CES-D 8 than those in the highest (the scale ranging from 0-24).
Critically, these associations are not uniform across national contexts.

The gender gap in depressive symptoms was larger in Southern European countries-particularly Portugal and Spain than in Northern and Eastern Europe, while the protective effect of higher income was strongest in Bulgaria, Hungary, Belgium, and Greece.

Country context alone accounted for only a small proportion of total variance in depressive symptoms (ICC = 0.033), indicating that differences in depression at the population level are driven primarily by sociodemographic factors, but that their magnitude is meaningfully shaped by where people live.

Depression is one of the leading causes of disability worldwide, affecting an estimated 332 million people globally (WHO, 2025), and 32.18 million people living in the EU -7.2% of the population in 2019 (Eurostat, 2021).
text.formatted: Depression is one of the leading causes of disability worldwide, affecting an estimated 332 million people globally (WHO, 2025), and 32.18 million people living in the EU -7.2% of the population in 2019 <ref type="bibr">(Eurostat, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms affect one in five adults across OECD and EU27 countries, and often go unrecognised and untreated, increasing the risk of progression to more severe conditions while increasing overall societal costs (OECD, 2025).

Consequences extend also beyond individual suffering: the economic burden of mental ill-health across the EU has been estimated at over €600 billion annually-equivalent to around 4% of EU GDP-driven primarily by reduced productivity, healthcare costs, and social welfare expenditure (European Parliament, 2023).

text.text: Policy responses that support the prevention and treatment of depression require reliable data.
Identifying who carries the greatest burden of depression, and how that varies across countries, is a prerequisite for designing effective and equitable interventions.

Evidence has accumulated that structural and economic factors-such as poverty, low income, unemployment, housing insecurity-are among the strongest drivers of depression and mental ill-health at the population level (Lund et al., 2018 , Ridley et al., 2020 , Talmatzky et al., 2026).

text.text: National income support programmes, for instance, have been shown to reduce depressive symptoms among low-income households (Lund et al., 2018), and the expansion of access to therapeutic interventions, such as the NHS' Talking Therapies, has demonstrated improvements in depression outcomes at scale (see NHS, n.d. for an overview of evaluations).

text.text: School-based mental health programmes targeting younger populations have been shown to be effective in reducing depressive symptoms and improving resilience across multiple European countries (OECD, 2025).
text.formatted: School-based mental health programmes targeting younger populations have been shown to be effective in reducing depressive symptoms and improving resilience across multiple European countries <ref type="bibr">(OECD, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Yet the design and targeting of such interventions depends critically on knowing which groups and which countries are most affected -and where the social determinants of depression operate most strongly.

The European Social Survey (ESS), a biennial cross-national probability survey of the resident population across Europe, has been one of the largest sources of comparable population-level data on depression on the continent.

Since 2006, several ESS rounds have included an eight-item short version of the Centre for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D 8), enabling consistent measurement of depressive symptom burden across a large and diverse set of countries using a single validated instrument and rigorous probability sampling.

The psychometric properties of the CES-D 8 in the ESS context have been established by Van de Velde et al. (2010a), who confirmed its validity, internal consistency, and cross-national measurement invariance across 25 European countries.

text.text: These analyses further showed that the magnitude of the gender gap in depression varies between countries (Van de Velde et al., 2013).
text.formatted: These analyses further showed that the magnitude of the gender gap in depression varies between countries (Van de <ref type="bibr">Velde et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Analyses based on earlier ESS rounds have documented consistent sociodemographic gradients in depression, with women reporting higher depression scores (Van de Velde et al., 2010b).
text.formatted: Analyses based on earlier ESS rounds have documented consistent sociodemographic gradients in depression, with women reporting higher depression scores (Van de <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Velde et al., 2010b)</ref>.

text.text: Data from the European Health Interview Survey (EHIS) also showed higher rates of clinical depression for those in lower socioeconomic positions, and certain age groups reporting higher depression scores (Arias-de la Torre et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Data from the European Health Interview Survey (EHIS) also showed higher rates of clinical depression for those in lower socioeconomic positions, and certain age groups reporting higher depression scores (Arias-de la <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Torre et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These previous ESS analyses were conducted on data from 2006, well before a series of developments that have substantially impacted the state of population mental health in Europe.
Two trends in particular are relevant.
First, there is growing evidence of a deterioration in overall mental health among younger people.
For many years, wellbeing data followed a U-shaped pattern by age -signaling higher well-being among the young and the old, with lower reported wellbeing in midlife.
This pattern could not be replicated in multiple studies since 2021, most recently in a 92-country study on well-being (Ruggeri et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This pattern could not be replicated in multiple studies since 2021, most recently in a 92-country study on well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Ruggeri et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: While this does not necessarily indicate we should expect a mirrored pattern for mental illness or depression specifically, these trends raise questions about whether the age gradient in depression documented in earlier ESS analyses remains accurate, and whether the population groups most in need of mental health support and policy consideration have shifted.
Second, the COVID-19 pandemic triggered one of the most significant disruptions to population mental health (and health in general) in recent history.

Global analyses estimate that the pandemic caused an almost 28% increase in the prevalence of major depression and a 26% increase in anxiety disorders worldwide in 2020 (COVID-19 Mental Disorders Collaborators, 2021).
text.formatted: Global analyses estimate that the pandemic caused an almost 28% increase in the prevalence of major depression and a 26% increase in anxiety disorders worldwide in 2020 <ref type="bibr">(COVID-19 Mental Disorders Collaborators, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: While some recovery has been documented as acute pandemic conditions subsided, the social and economic consequences of the pandemic-including elevated unemployment, rising costs of living, and growing income inequality-have continued to shape population mental health, and their effects have been unevenly distributed across sociodemographic groups.

Whether the sociodemographic gradients in depression established in earlier ESS rounds have persisted, widened, or shifted in the post-pandemic period is therefore an important and, as of now, unanswered question.

This paper uses ESS Round 11 data from 23 European countries (n = 39,645) to address three related issues to inform the European Commission's (2023) Comprehensive Approach to Mental Health through five specific research questions.
First, we assess how depressive symptoms are distributed across sociodemographic groups and countries in post-pandemic Europe.
Second, we explore to what extent country-level factors account for variation in depression, and what the average individual-level effects of gender, age, education, and income are across countries.
Third, we analyse how the effects of gender and income on depression vary across national contexts, and identify where these associations are strongest and weakest.
To address these questions, we use multilevel modelling to account for the cross-national nature of the data.

In doing so, we provide an update to the pre-pandemic evidence base on depression in Europe, and contribute to the growing evidence on which population groups and national contexts should be prioritised for mental health investment.
What is the weighted prevalence and distribution of depressive symptoms (CES-D 8) across 23 European countries in ESS Round 11?
How do depressive symptoms vary by gender, age group, education level, and income across countries?
RQ3.
What proportion of the total variance in depressive symptoms is attributable to country-level factors (ICC)?
What are the average individual-level effects of gender, age, education, and income on depressive symptoms across all 23 countries simultaneously (M1 -fixed effects model)?
RQ5.

Do the effects of gender and income on depressive symptoms vary significantly across national contexts (M2 -random slopes model), and if so, in which countries are these effects strongest and weakest?

The inclusion of specific sociodemographic predictors in this analysis-gender, age, education, and income-follows from both prior theoretical and empirical work and their distinct policy relevance, as outlined above.
Data were drawn from Round 11 of the ESS collected between 2023 and 2024.
The ESS is a biennial cross-national survey that uses strict probability sampling of the resident population aged 15 and above in each participating country.
Full methodological documentation is available from the ESS website (www.europeansocialsurvey.org).
text.formatted: Full methodological documentation is available from the ESS website (<ref type="url" target="www.europeansocialsurvey.org">www.europeansocialsurvey.org</ref>).

text.text: The analytical sample comprised all 22 EU countries that participated in round 11 (+ the UK) and included the health inequalities module containing the CES-D 8, namely: Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, UK, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, and Sweden.
The UK is included in addition to EU countries in line with the overall approach of the Resilient and Mentally Healthy Societies (REMESOS) project, which this paper is part of.

After excluding respondents with fewer than six valid CES-D 8-item responses-requiring completion of at least 75% of scale items-the total analytical sample comprised 39,645 individuals (n = 169 excluded).

The analysis plan was pre-registered on the Open Science Framework prior to analysis [ Annex 1; timestamped PR to be made public upon acceptance]; the analysis was conducted in R; the code is available for review and reproduction.
Depressive symptoms were measured using the CES-D 8, an eight-item short form of the Centre for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (Radloff, 1977).
text.formatted: Depressive symptoms were measured using the CES-D 8, an eight-item short form of the Centre for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Radloff, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: The items assess the frequency of depressive symptoms in the past week, including depressed mood, lack of energy, restless sleep, loneliness, sadness, difficulty getting going, and-worded positively-happiness, and enjoyment of life.
Responses follow a four-point scale from 1 ("all or most of the time") to 4 ("none of the time"), which are rescored 0-3 for analysis (Beller et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Responses follow a four-point scale from 1 ("all or most of the time") to 4 ("none of the time"), which are rescored 0-3 for analysis <ref type="bibr">(Beller et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The two positively worded items were reverse-scored prior to summing, so that higher scores consistently reflect greater symptom frequency.
Total scores ranged from 0 to 24, with higher values indicating more frequent depressive symptoms.

While some have attempted to use the CES-D 8-item version with a threshold to indicate the onset of clinical depression (Beller et al., 2021), the tool generally lacks an established clinical cut-off point (Van de Velde et al., 2010b) -unlike, for example, various versions of the PHQ, or the full 20-item version of the CES-D itself (Radloff, 1977).

text.text: The validity, internal consistency, and cross-national measurement invariance of the CES-D 8 in the ESS have been established by Van de Velde et al. (2010a), who confirmed adequate psychometric properties across 25 European countries and found a one-dimensional factor structure to be the best-fitting model.

(2010a)</ref>, who confirmed adequate psychometric properties across 25 European countries and found a one-dimensional factor structure to be the best-fitting model.

text.text: The use of a sum score as the outcome in multilevel models is consistent with this established factor structure and with prior ESS-based analyses, and is appropriate for an epidemiological research context where a simple, interpretable measure of symptom frequency is the primary interest.
Four sociodemographic predictors were included: gender, age, education, and income.

These were selected on the basis of prior theoretical and empirical work on the determinants of depression (Lorant et al., 2003 , Van de Velde et al., 2010b) and pre-specified in the analysis pre-registration.
text.formatted: These were selected on the basis of prior theoretical and empirical work on the determinants of depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Lorant et al., 2003</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">, Van de Velde et al., 2010b)</ref> and pre-specified in the analysis pre-registration.

text.text: All predictors are treated as confounders of each other's associations with depression; no mediating variables are included.
All four predictors are included as covariates without imposing a causal ordering.

Given that plausible pathways exist in multiple directions among gender, age, education, income, and depression (e.g. depression affecting occupational attainment and income; income shaping access to resources that buffer depression), and given the cross-sectional study design, we treat the resulting coefficients as descriptive conditional associations rather than causal estimates.
Gender was coded as male (reference category) or female.
Age was grouped into seven categories consistent with ESS standards: 15-24 (reference category), 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65-74, and 75 and older.

Education was operationalised as three levels following the International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED): low (ISCED 0-2: up to lower secondary education; reference category), medium (ISCED 3-4: upper secondary and post-secondary, but non-tertiary education), and high (ISCED 5-8: Tertiary education, any university education up to doctoral degrees or equivalent).
Household income was measured using the ESS ten-decile scale per country (hinctnta) and grouped into three categories: low (deciles 1-3, reference), middle (deciles 4-7), and high (deciles 8-10).
Missing value codes were recoded to missing for all variables prior to analysis and handled via listwise deletion in regression models.
Missing data on predictor variables resulted in the exclusion of 8,677 individuals (21.9%) from regression models via listwise deletion, yielding a multilevel model sample of n = 30,968.

Missingness was driven almost entirely by non-response on the household income measure (n = 8,399 missing), with minimal missing data on education (n = 242) and age (n = 263), and no missing data on gender.

Given the potential non-random nature of income non-response-those with missing income may systematically differ from those who reported it-results from the multilevel models should be interpreted with this in mind (see limitations section).

All descriptive analyses used the ESS analytical weight (anweight), which corrects for differential selection probabilities within countries, non-response, non-coverage, and differences in population size across countries, enabling comparable weighted estimates across national contexts (Kaminska, 2020).

text.text: The full sample design-including clustering (primary sampling units) and stratification-was accounted for in all descriptive analyses.
This approach follows the ESS weighting guidelines (Kaminska, 2020) for producing nationally and cross-nationally representative estimates.
text.formatted: This approach follows the ESS weighting guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Kaminska, 2020)</ref> for producing nationally and cross-nationally representative estimates.

text.text: For the multilevel model, anweight was scaled within each country to a mean of 1.

This preserves within-country variation in selection probabilities while preventing countries with larger populations from disproportionately influencing the model estimates -a standard approach in weighted multilevel analysis of cross-national survey data (Rabe-Hesketh & Skrondal, 2006).

The analysis proceeded in two stages.
First, we computed weighted means and 95% confidence intervals for CES-D 8 scores by country and by each sociodemographic subgroup.
These descriptive estimates used the survey-weighted design-based procedures appropriate for complex probability samples.
Second, we estimated three multilevel models of increasing complexity, with country as the second level.

We deemed multilevel modelling the most appropriate analytical framework here because individuals are nested within countries -meaning that people in the same country are more likely to be similar to each other than to those in other countries, due to shared social, economic, and cultural conditions.
Standard regression ignores this clustering and risks underestimating standard errors, potentially producing misleading statistical inference.

Multilevel models explicitly partition the variation in depression into individual-level and country-level components, and allow both average effects and cross-national variation in those effects to be estimated simultaneously.
The null model (M0) included no predictors and a random intercept for country, and was estimated using restricted maximum likelihood (REML).

Its purpose was to compute the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), which expresses the proportion of total variance in CES-D 8 scores attributable to country-level factors rather than individual differences.

A low ICC indicates that most variation in depression lies between individuals within countries rather than between countries, but does not preclude meaningful cross-national variation in sociodemographic gradients.
where γ₀₀ is the grand mean, u₀ⱼ ~ N(0, τ₀₀) is the random intercept for country j, and εᵢⱼ ~ N(0, σ²) is the individual-level residual.
The fixed effects model (M1) added all four sociodemographic predictors as fixed effects alongside the random intercept, and was estimated using maximum likelihood (ML) to allow model comparison.

This model estimates the average association of each predictor with depressive symptoms across all 23 countries simultaneously, while adjusting for all other predictors and accounting for the clustering of individuals within countries, which induces non-independence of observations sharing the same national context.
The resulting coefficients represent the expected difference in CES-D 8 score associated with each predictor category, relative to the reference group, averaged across the full sample.

CES-D8ᵢⱼ = γ₀₀ + γ₁₀Genderᵢⱼ + γ₂₀Ageᵢⱼ + γ₃₀Educationᵢⱼ + γ₄₀Incomeᵢⱼ + u₀ⱼ + εᵢⱼ where γ₁₀ through γ₄₀ are fixed effects representing average associations of each predictor with CES-D 8 across all countries, and u₀ⱼ is the random intercept for country j.
The random slopes model (M2) allows the effects of gender and income to vary randomly across countries, alongside the random intercept.

This model tests whether the relationship between gender and depression, as well as between income and depression, differs across national contexts -that is, whether the gender gap and the income gradient are larger in some countries than others.
Country-specific slope estimates (best linear unbiased predictors, or BLUPs) were extracted from M2 and visualised to illustrate cross-national variation in each gradient.
M1 and M2 were compared using a likelihood ratio test.
The large sample size gives the test high statistical power to detect even small improvements in fit.
We also report differences in AIC and BIC as complementary fit indicators.

As income is a three-level ordinal variable, M2 estimates two random slopes-for middle versus low income and for high versus low income-along with their covariances with the random intercept and gender slope.

CES-D8ᵢⱼ = γ₀₀ + (γ₁₀ + u₁ⱼ)Genderᵢⱼ + γ₂₀Ageᵢⱼ + γ₃₀Educationᵢⱼ + (γ₄₀ + u₂ⱼ)Incomeᵢⱼ + u₀ⱼ + εᵢⱼ where u₁ⱼ ~ N(0, τ₁₁) is the random slope for gender and u₂ⱼ ~ N(0, τ₂₂) is the random slope for income, both varying across countries.
Country-specific slope estimates (BLUPs) are extracted from M2 and visualised as forest plots showing country variation in the gender gap and income gradient.
All analyses were conducted in R using the survey package for weighted descriptives and the lme4 and lmerTest packages for multilevel modelling.
The reference category throughout all analyses is males, aged 15-24, with low education (ISCED 0-2), and low income (deciles 1-3).

The direction of the effect was consistent, but its magnitude differed.
Bulgaria (-2.68), Hungary (-2.06), Belgium (-1.97), and Greece (-1.96) showed the steepest gradients, meaning that the depression burden associated with low income was most severe in these countries.

Ireland (-0.52), Slovakia (-0.70), and the UK (-0.76) showed the weakest gradients, suggesting that structural factors may buffer some of the mental health consequences of low income in these contexts.

Country comparisons were broadly consistent at the steeper end: Hungary (-4.19) and Bulgaria (-4.06) again showed the steepest gradients, yet the protective effect of high income in Hungary was considerably larger then between low and middle income.
In Spain, the association between high versus low income and depressive symptoms was comparatively small (-1.14), as was the case in Sweden (-1.19) and Poland (-1.25).
The pattern of cross-national variation was broadly consistent with that observed for the middle vs low income contrast, though some notable differences emerged.

In Slovakia, the difference between low and middle income groups was relatively small, whereas the difference between low and high income groups was considerably larger (-2.35), suggesting that income-related differences in depressive symptoms are more pronounced at the extremes of the income distribution.

text.text: To assess whether allowing the effects of gender and income to vary across countries improved model fit, we compared M1 against M2 using a likelihood ratio test.

text.text: The significant likelihood ratio test should therefore be interpreted cautiously, given the large sample size, which gives the test high power to detect even negligible improvements in fit.

Nonetheless, the country-specific slope estimates from M2 confirm meaningful variation in the strength of the gender and income gradients across national contexts, which the fixed effects model cannot capture.

Firstly, and most critically, this study does not make causal claims.

While causal inference approaches can in principle be applied to cross-sectional survey data, they require strong theoretical assumptions about the causal structure of the predictors and the availability of suitable instruments.
The four predictors included in this analysis-gender, age, education, and incomeare plausibly related to one another through multiple causal pathways.
For instance, education shapes income -or vice versa.
Depression may, in turn, reduce income-earning capacity.

For this investigation, we were interested in identifying how depression varies across these sociodemographic variables to inform policy on the strength of their influence and differences between countries.

Missing data on predictor variables, driven almost entirely by non-response on the household income measure (n = 8,399 missing, 21.2% of the analytical sample), resulted in the exclusion of 8,677 individuals from regression models via listwise deletion, yielding a multilevel model sample of n = 30,968.

Given the likely non-random nature of income non-response, we conducted a sensitivity check by re-estimating M1 excluding income as a predictor on both the full analytical sample (n = 39,645) and the listwise-deleted sample (n = 30,968), so that any differences in the remaining coefficients would reflect sample composition rather than the effect of income itself.
Gender and education coefficients were stable across both samples, suggesting listwise deletion did not materially bias estimates for these predictors.

However, age coefficients were somewhat larger in the full sample, most notably for those aged 75 and over, whose scores were on average 2.20 points higher than the 15-24 reference group in the full sample, compared to 1.63 points in the restricted sample, suggesting that older respondents are disproportionately represented among those with missing income data.
Estimates for age in the main models should therefore be interpreted with some caution.
While we followed standards set by the ESS for age grouping, which are frequently employed in investigations using its data, age grouping by default comes with some level of arbitrariness.

We identified one particular concern, which is that the youngest age group mixes young people often still in mandatory educational settings (15-17) with people who are predominantly free to choose between continued education, vocational training, or work.

However, integrating a separate group of 15-to 17-year-olds into analysis was unfeasible due to the small number of participants in that age group (ranging from a maximum of 69 in Germany to a minimum of 5 in Cyprus).

In a descriptive analysis splitting the group at that age across the entire sample, however, we find that the group of 18-24 still scores below average on the CES-D and can therefore conclude they are not the sole driver of lower depression scores in the young age group as applied in our analysis.
A further limitation concerns the absence of a validated clinical cut-off for the CES-D 8 as scored in the ESS context, i.e. a score that indicates the presence or absence of clinical depression.
While the scale has well-established psychometric properties and is widely used as a continuous measure of depressive symptom burden, no consensus cut-off exists for the 0-24 scoring used here.

The majority of ESS-based studies using the CES-D 8 rely exclusively on continuous scores (Van de Velde et al., 2010a Velde et al., , 2010b)), and the one ESS study that applied a binary threshold used a cut-off of >9 to indicate 'at-risk' depression, explicitly does not make a clinical interpretation (Beller et al., 2021).

text.text: As a result, we report the distribution of depressive symptoms as a continuous outcome and do not estimate clinical prevalence.
This limits how much numerical differences can be translated into tangible interpretations of burden of disease.
Future work should consider developing and validating a cut-off appropriate for this instrument and scoring convention in general population samples across Europe.

Finally, the dataset in question contains 22 of 27 EU countries, meaning there is no comparable data for Czechia, Denmark, Luxembourg, Malta, and Romania, for which no data were available at the time the data were downloaded (February 2026).

This study provides an updated picture of the sociodemographic patterning of depressive symptoms across Europe, using ESS Round 11 data collected in 2023-24 -nearly two decades after the analyses conducted by Van de Velde and colleagues on ESS Round 3 (2006-07).
The findings confirm the persistence of several well-established gradients while also revealing shifts in their magnitude and distribution.

Income emerged as the strongest individual-level predictor of depressive symptoms, with those in the lowest income tertile scoring on average 2.09 points higher on the CES-D 8 than those in the highest tertile after adjusting for gender, age, and education.
This aligns with an extensive body of evidence linking economic hardship to common mental disorders (Lund et al., 2018; Lorant et al., 2003) and to depression specifically (Kersjes et al. 2025).

text.text: The strength of the income gradient relative to education and gender suggests that policies targeting income adequacy and poverty reduction may have the greatest potential for reducing the population burden of depressive symptoms.
Critically, the income gradient is not uniform across Europe.
The association between low income and depression was most pronounced in Hungary and Bulgaria, and comparatively modest in Ireland, Slovakia, and the UK.

Notably, a population-level investigation from Germany (N = 92,267) found a strong increase in the gap between clinically relevant depression cases between high and low-income groups (Kersjes et al. 2025), indicating the need for this to be further monitored across countries.

text.text: The comparatively low ICC in the current study nonetheless reinforces that individual sociodemographic characteristics-particularly income-account for the strongest differences in depressive symptom burden across Europe.

This finding has a clear implication for the use of population strategies (Rose, 1985) to reduce depression: interventions targeting individual-level risk factors are likely to have greater population-level impact than country-level structural interventions alone.
text.formatted: This finding has a clear implication for the use of population strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Rose, 1985)</ref> to reduce depression: interventions targeting individual-level risk factors are likely to have greater population-level impact than country-level structural interventions alone.

text.text: Low income is a particularly difficult factor to influence for most policymakers, as they a) can rarely simply provide additional funds to people and b) this likely would not solve the complex issues through which low income can increase depression.

However, identifying who is most impacted within this group and pathways through which low income increases depression can inform strategies, such as increasing the availability of therapy or creating opportunities for communities to connect if a major driver is loneliness.

While low income and gender affect depression across almost all countries, cultural context should not be ignored in addressing them -either in policy (Ruggeri et al., 2021), mental health promotion more generally (Naeim & Basharpoor, 2026), or treatment (Kirmayer, 2012).

text.text: The random slopes model demonstrated that the associations between gender, income, and depression vary meaningfully across countries.
The same individual-level risk factor-being female, or being in the lowest income group-thus carries different implications for depressive symptoms depending on where a person lives.
As such, policy responses that treat all countries equally risk overlooking crucial differences.

For example, while Latvia and Lithuania score higher than almost all countries on average, there appears to be no difference in depression levels between men and women, whereas Portugal also scores higher than average generally, but shows the largest difference between the two groups, making gender focused policy likely impactful in the latter country, but not in the other two and definitely warrants country-level investigation.
The gender gap in depressive symptoms remains.
Women scored on average 0.77 points higher than men on the CES-D 8 in the current study, compared to a regression coefficient of 0.81 points reported for 2006-2007.
The gap remains statistically robust and near-universal across countries.
The broad regional pattern also persists: Portugal, Spain, Cyprus, and Italy show the largest gender gaps.

This is consistent with Van de Velde et al.'s (2013) finding that macro-level gender equality-particularly equality in power over economic resources and political participation-is associated with smaller gender differences in depression, and that Southern European countries, which score comparatively lower on these dimensions, tend to show larger gaps.

(2021), analysing ESS rounds from 2006 to 2014, found that depressive symptoms declined across all age groups over that period, but the improvement was weakest among younger adults and strongest among older adults -a difference they partly attributed to improvements in income, education, and health among the latter.

text.text: In the current data, the 25-34 age group reports elevated symptoms relative to the youngest reference category, and the oldest group (75+) records the highest symptom burden of any age group.

The improvement in older adults documented through 2014 appears not to have been sustained into the post-pandemic period, in which older populations faced disproportionate social isolation and healthcare disruption.
These findings carry several implications for policy, particularly the European Commission's Comprehensive Approach to Mental Health (European Commission, 2023).

text.text: The magnitude and cross-national variation of the income gradient point to economic policy as a primary lever for reducing depression.

Countries where the association between low income and depression is most pronounced-particularly Hungary and Bulgaria-may require more intensive income support mechanisms alongside investment in mental healthcare and treatment.
The persistent gender gap, and its variation across countries, reinforces Van de Velde et al.'s (2013) argument that gender equality is a structural determinant of mental health.
text.formatted: The persistent gender gap, and its variation across countries, reinforces Van de <ref type="bibr">Velde et al.'s (2013)</ref> argument that gender equality is a structural determinant of mental health.

text.text: Progress on formal equality indicators may not be sufficient if economic and resource-based inequalities between men and women persist, particularly in Southern European countries, where the gap remains largest.

The elevated depressive symptoms among the 25-34 age group, alongside the well-documented deterioration in youth mental health across Europe, suggest that age-targeted prevention strategies for young adults navigating labour market entry in conditions of economic uncertainty warrant prioritisation.

The Commission's approach addresses youth mental health, but the current findings suggest that early adulthood-not only adolescence-is a critical window for intervention, when it comes to depression specifically.
In the long-term, such strategies will only remain truly successful within an economy that creates meaningful work opportunities that pay livable wages.
Finally, as Van de Velde et al. (2013) concluded, focusing solely on top-level average European benchmarks will not be sufficient.

text.text: The differences in both the income gradient and the gender gap between countries indicate that effective mental health policy should simultaneously consider the structural determinants of depression at both the individual and national level, and not disregard national contexts when building EU wide responses.

• Step 1: Missing value codes (7, 8, 9) are recoded to NA across all eight items.

• Step 2: The two positively worded items -wrhpp (was happy) and enjlf (enjoyed life)are reverse scored using the transformation 5 -raw score, so that higher scores on all items consistently indicate greater depressive symptom frequency.

Missing Data Missing value codes on CES-D 8 items (7, 8, 9) are recoded to NA prior to scoring.
Respondents with fewer than six valid items are excluded from CES-D 8 analyses.
Missing data on predictor variables are recoded to NA and handled via listwise deletion in regression models.
The number of respondents excluded from each analysis is reported.
No imputation is applied.
Missing at random (MAR) is assumed.
Statistical Inference The significance threshold is set at α = .05 for all primary analyses.
No correction for multiple testing is applied across subgroup comparisons, which are treated as descriptive.
The likelihood ratio test comparing M1 and M2 is the primary inferential test.
Causal Assumptions This is an observational secondary analysis and no causal claims are made.
Gender, age, education, and income are specified as confounders of each other's associations with depressive symptoms.
Unmeasured country-level factors -including welfare state regime, gender equality indices, and macroeconomic conditions -may confound between-country associations and are acknowledged as limitations.
Random slope estimates from M2 are descriptive and do not support causal inference about country-level moderators.

text.text: Background and Rationale Prior research using earlier ESS waves has documented consistent gender and socioeconomic gradients in depressive symptoms, as well as substantial cross-national variation in their prevalence and social determinants (Van de Velde et al., 2010; Van de Velde et al., 2013).
However, this evidence base largely predates the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent shifts in population mental health, economic conditions, and social inequality across Europe.
ESS Round 11 (2023-24) provides the most recent comparable cross-national data on depressive symptoms using the CES-D 8, covering 23 European countries.

This study uses these data to update and extend prior cross-national research on the social determinants of depression, examining both the average individual-level effects of gender, age, education, and income and the extent to which these effects vary across national contexts.
